title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I look at median household income across counties in New York, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                         myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                         <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 36001 Albany County, New York       83149   1788  315374    NA
2 36003 Allegany County, New York     61233   2429   47027    NA
3 36005 Bronx County, New York        49036    872 1419250    NA
4 36007 Broome County, New York       61059   1769  197738    NA
5 36009 Cattaraugus County, New York  58248   1978   76479    NA
6 36011 Cayuga County, New York       66583   2266   75464    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         53        369308.
2 Moderate                 9         33224.


[What is the average population of high-confidence counties versus low-confidence counties? Is there a pattern?] The average population for for high-confidence counties is 369307.62 versus the moderate which is 33223.89. Yes, there is pattern - counties with larger population have high confidence while counties with lower population have low-confidence. —
[Your 200–250 word reflection goes here.] We know the least about Hamilton County, Schuyler County and Yates County out of the 62 counties in the state of New York. And this is due to due to their smaller population number. Things could go wrong in many subsidy allocation when building public infrastructure such as road, electricity and housing. And that could affect how people live, play and work and most of all; their access to opportunities could be dramatically limited. —

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Alfred Lubrano’s 2018 WHYY article reports that Eastwick’s poverty rate rose from 12% to 26% and Holmesburg’s from 2% to 19%. I wanted to see how much of the reported change is clear once I account for uncertainty in the ACS estimates.
I use Philadelphia census tracts from the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 ACS five-year surveys. These periods do not overlap. I calculate poverty rates using B17001_002 (people below poverty) divided by B17001_001 (people whose poverty status was determined). The article does not list the tracts used for each neighborhood, so I test tract-level changes rather than reproduce its neighborhood figures.


Show code
phillypoverty_2010 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  state = "PA",
  county= "Philadelphia",
  year = 2010,
variables = c(
    total_pop=
      "B17001_001",
    poverty_pop =
      "B17001_002"
  ),survey = "acs5"
  )

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
What does the evidence support?
Supported: I found detectable poverty-rate changes in some Philadelphia census tracts. Of the 376 tracts I could compare, 36 had an increase and 27 had a decrease at 90% confidence.
Cannot be determined: I cannot check the article’s exact numbers for Eastwick, Holmesburg, or Fairhill with the tract data I used. The article gives neighborhood figures but does not say which tracts were included in each neighborhood. I would be guessing if I assigned tracts to those names. My calculations also cover poverty among everyone in the poverty measure, so they cannot test the article’s discussion of white poverty.
Not supported: My results do not support reading the article as evidence that poverty rates clearly rose across most Philadelphia tracts. Only 36 of the 376 tracts had a detectable increase; 27 had a detectable decrease, and 313 had no detectable change. That does not mean the article’s Eastwick or Holmesburg figures are wrong. My tract analysis cannot settle those neighborhood claims.

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Rewrite
Philadelphia’s poverty rates did not move in one clear direction across the city. Comparing the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 surveys, I found detectable increases in 36 census tracts and detectable decreases in 27. In 313 other tracts, the data did not establish whether poverty changed. These results show why a large estimated jump should be checked against its margin of error before calling it a clear increase. The article reports increases for Eastwick and Holmesburg, but without its neighborhood boundaries, I cannot verify those specific figures from tract data.

check_na <- function(formula, df) {
  vars <- all.vars(formula[[3]])
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1).")
  }
}

# Same folds, with prediction safeguards learned from each training fold.
cv_cache <- new.env()
guard_features <- function(newdata, training, formula) {
  vars <- all.vars(formula[[3]])
  for (v in vars) if (is.numeric(training[[v]])) {
    bounds <- range(training[[v]],na.rm=TRUE)
    newdata[[v]] <- pmax(bounds[1],pmin(bounds[2],newdata[[v]]))
  }
  newdata
}
cv_fit <- function(formula, data) {
  key <- paste(deparse(formula),collapse="")
  if (!exists(key,cv_cache,inherits=FALSE)) {
    d <- st_drop_geometry(data)
    check_na(formula,d)
    set.seed(5080)
    folds <- caret::createFolds(d$sale_price,k=10,returnTrain=TRUE)
    pred <- rep(NA_real_,nrow(d)); rmse <- numeric(10)
    for (i in seq_along(folds)) {
      tr <- folds[[i]]; val <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(d)),tr)
      model <- lm(formula,data=d[tr,])
      heldout <- guard_features(d[val,],d[tr,],formula)
      pred[val] <- pmax(0,predict(model,newdata=heldout))
      rmse[i] <- sqrt(mean((d$sale_price[val]-pred[val])^2))
    }
    assign(key,list(results=data.frame(RMSE=mean(rmse)),pred=data.frame(rowIndex=seq_len(nrow(d)),pred=pred)),cv_cache)
  }
  get(key,cv_cache)
}
cv_rmse <- function(formula,data) cv_fit(formula,data)$results$RMSE
cv_pred <- function(formula,data) cv_fit(formula,data)$pred$pred

# Chicago Data Portal (Socrata) -> sf. `where` is a SoQL filter.
socrata_get <- function(dataset, where, select = NULL, limit = 200000) {
  where <- str_squish(where)
  q <- paste0("$where=", URLencode(where, reserved = TRUE), "&$limit=", limit)
  if (!is.null(select)) q <- paste0(q, "&$select=", URLencode(str_squish(select), reserved = TRUE))
  url <- paste0("https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/", dataset, ".geojson?", q)
  tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".geojson")
  resp <- tryCatch(download.file(url, tmp, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) e)
  if (inherits(resp, "error")) stop("Portal request failed. Open this URL in a browser to see why:\n", url)
  st_read(tmp, quiet = TRUE)
}

  df$dist_train_mi <- nearest_miles(train_stops)
  df$dist_bus_mi <- nearest_miles(bus_stops)
  df$dist_bike_mi <- nearest_miles(bikes)
  buffers <- st_buffer(df,dist=1320)
  df$parks_radius <- lengths(st_intersects(buffers,parks))
  crime_date <- as.Date(lubridate::mdy_hms(crimes$Date,quiet=TRUE))
  nearby <- st_intersects(buffers,crimes)
  sold <- as.Date(lubridate::mdy(df$sale_date,quiet=TRUE))
  df$crime_radius <- vapply(seq_along(nearby),function(i) as.integer(sum(crime_date[nearby[[i]]]<sold[i],na.rm=TRUE)),integer(1))
  nn_afd <- st_nn(df,afd_housing,k=5,returnDist=FALSE,progress=FALSE)
  df$mean_afdHousing <- vapply(nn_afd,function(i) mean(afd_housing$Units[i],na.rm=TRUE),numeric(1))
  df$afdHousing_radius <- lengths(st_intersects(buffers,afd_housing))
  df$in_ADU_area <- lengths(st_intersects(df,ADU))>0
  # Use the supplied community polygons; retain unassigned homes as Unknown.
  df <- st_join(df,comm_area %>% select(community=COMMUNITY),largest=TRUE) %>%
    mutate(community=factor(replace_na(community,"Unknown")))
  clean_train <- df[match(clean_train$id,df$id),]
}

Answer: What in your exploration shaped your modeling choices?
Your answer:
First, the dependent variable is extremely skewed. There are very few houses that sell for many times the price of a median house and very few that are sold at extremely low prices. We excluded the log-price tails for this model, but unusual prices are not necessarily non-market transactions, so this choice limits generalization. Furthermore, the continuous variables that were highly skewed were logged to better fulfill linear regression assumptions.
Second, pairwise plots alone cannot rule out multicollinearity, and some categorical features may be redundant. Interaction effects should be tested out. There are also a lot of variables to add, which means a stepwise regression would be beneficial for variable selection.
Lastly, house sales price are clustered depending on location. The Northeast end seems to have a higher sale prices. Adding a fixed effect variable will be useful for accounting for this.

moran <- function(formula, df, response, k = 5) {
  rmse <- cv_rmse(formula, df)
  pred <- cv_pred(formula, df)
  resid_cv <- df[[response]] - pred
  
  coords <- st_coordinates(df)
  
  w_knn <- nb2listw(knn2nb(knearneigh(st_coordinates(df), k = k)), style = "W")
  
  moran_res <- moran.test(resid_cv , w_knn)
  moran_i <- moran_res$estimate[["Moran I statistic"]]
  moran_p <- moran_res$p.value
  
  tibble(
    moran_i = moran_i,
    moran_p = moran_p
  )
}

Answer: What helped most, and what disappointed you? Use your log.
Your answer:
The model log records each trial in order. In every validation fold, numeric predictors are limited to that fold’s training range and predictions are floored at zero. The same rule is used for final test predictions to prevent extreme extrapolation, especially from very small lots. This safeguard does not guarantee accurate prices for unusual homes. The largest one-step improvement came from m13: community. Baseline CV RMSE was $219,610; the final selected formula has CV RMSE $135,451. Community effects allow prices to differ across Chicago. Transit and affordable-housing features should be judged by the log; their coefficients are associations, not causal effects.
Stepwise selection used all retained training rows before CV. Its CV score is conditional on that selected formula and may be optimistic. Nested selection is needed to validate the full selection procedure. Repeated sales can also occur across random CV folds, unlike the instructor’s house-level test split.

Part 6: Reflection (about 300 words, as a team)

Read one coefficient twice: once as β̂, once for what it does to ŷ.
Would you hand this model to the Assessor? What would you warn them about?

Your answer:
Our model keeps sale price in dollars and combines house features with location. Age class C starts at 50 years in our code, and class A is below 20. The class C coefficient compares those age groups while holding other model terms constant. It should not be described as a comparison of homes above 60 years.
We read the bus-distance coefficient in two ways. Its fitted coefficient is 53778.14 dollars per mile. For the prediction, moving from 0.1 to 0.2 miles from a bus stop changes the fitted value by $5377.81, holding the other terms constant. This is a conditional association. It does not show that moving a stop would cause that price change. With the size-by-community interaction, a 10% increase in building size changes the prediction by log(1.10) times that community’s size slope.
We would not hand this model to the Assessor for direct use yet. The final CV score estimates error on retained training sales, while the instructor’s test prices are still withheld. Selection before CV and repeated sales across folds can make that estimate optimistic. The income ratio table matters because households can face different relative errors even when overall RMSE improves.
Our cleaning rule also needs caution: it identifies unusual prices, not verified non-market sales. It removes some low-value homes that matter most for the fairness question. Crime counts use only events before each sale, but early 2023 has less observation history. The supplied amenity files lack historical snapshot dates. We would first verify those dates, review excluded sales, use property-grouped validation, and test the entire selection process inside the folds. More complex models could be compared later, but improved accuracy must be demonstrated. Interpretability is useful; it does not make an estimate fair or ready to set tax bills.
